title: Cloud Deployment
description: Deploy your ASP.NET Core application to the cloud using Azure App Service and Azure CLI. Learn to create resource groups, provision App Service plans, deploy with Git or ZIP deploy, and use deployment slots for safe releases.

blocks.text: Cloud deployment moves your application from a server you manage to a platform managed by a cloud provider. Azure App Service is Microsoft's managed platform for web applications. You deploy your code, and Azure handles the operating system, runtime updates, scaling, SSL certificates, and high availability. This lets you focus on your application rather than infrastructure.

Azure App Service supports ASP.NET Core natively. You can deploy via Git, ZIP deploy, Docker containers, or directly from Visual Studio. The platform automatically detects your application type, provisions the runtime, and starts it. You can scale up (more powerful VMs) or scale out (more instances) with a single API call or portal click.

Azure organizes resources into a hierarchy. A Resource Group is a logical container that holds related resources. An App Service Plan defines the compute resources (CPU, memory, VM size) that your apps run on. Multiple apps can share a single App Service Plan, splitting the cost. The Web App is your actual application running inside the plan.

blocks.title: Azure App Service Resource Hierarchy
items: Subscription: Your billing boundary — all Azure resources belong to a subscription
Resource Group: A logical container for related resources — one app, its database, and storage
App Service Plan: Defines the compute tier (Free, Basic, Standard, Premium) and VM size
Web App: Your actual ASP.NET Core application running on the plan
Deployment Slot: A staging environment for the same app — swap slots with zero downtime

blocks.text: The Azure CLI is a cross-platform command-line tool for managing Azure resources. You can script the entire infrastructure setup — resource groups, app service plans, web apps, databases — making your deployment reproducible and suitable for CI/CD pipelines.

blocks.title: Install Azure CLI
blocks.text: Install Azure CLI from https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cli/azure/install-azure-cli. Once installed, run az login to authenticate with your Azure account before running deployment commands.

blocks.title: Deploying an ASP.NET Core App with Azure CLI
blocks.content: Complete Azure CLI commands to create a resource group, app service plan, web app, and deploy your application.
blocks.code:
# 1. Log in to Azure (opens a browser window)
az login

# 2. Create a resource group (a logical container for resources)
az group create \
  --name MyResourceGroup \
  --location eastus

# 3. Create an App Service Plan (defines compute tier)
az appservice plan create \
  --name MyAppPlan \
  --resource-group MyResourceGroup \
  --sku B1 \
  --is-linux

# 4. Create the Web App
az webapp create \
  --name MyWebApp12345 \
  --resource-group MyResourceGroup \
  --plan MyAppPlan \
  --runtime "DOTNETCORE:8.0"

# 5. Deploy using ZIP deploy (publish locally first)
dotnet publish MyApp.csproj --configuration Release --output ./publish
cd publish
zip -r ../app.zip .
az webapp deploy \
  --resource-group MyResourceGroup \
  --name MyWebApp12345 \
  --src-path ../app.zip \
  --type zip

# 6. Configure an app setting (connection string)
az webapp config connection-string set \
  --resource-group MyResourceGroup \
  --name MyWebApp12345 \
  --connection-string-type SQLAzure \
  --settings DefaultConnection="Server=tcp:...;..."

blocks.text: Deployment slots are live applications with their own hostnames, deployed alongside your production app. You deploy to a staging slot, test it thoroughly, and then swap it with the production slot. The swap operation is near-instantaneous and warms up the new code before it receives live traffic, minimizing downtime.

blocks.title: Creating and Swapping Deployment Slots
blocks.content: Using Azure CLI to create a staging slot and swap it into production.
blocks.code:
# Create a staging deployment slot
az webapp deployment slot create \
  --resource-group MyResourceGroup \
  --name MyWebApp12345 \
  --slot staging

# Deploy to staging (not production)
az webapp deploy \
  --resource-group MyResourceGroup \
  --name MyWebApp12345 \
  --slot staging \
  --src-path ./app.zip \
  --type zip

# Configure slot-specific settings (e.g., connection strings)
az webapp config connection-string set \
  --resource-group MyResourceGroup \
  --name MyWebApp12345 \
  --slot staging \
  --connection-string-type SQLAzure \
  --settings DefaultConnection="Server=staging-db;..."

# Swap staging into production (zero-downtime swap)
az webapp deployment slot swap \
  --resource-group MyResourceGroup \
  --name MyWebApp12345 \
  --slot staging \
  --target-slot production

# After the swap, the old production code is in 'staging'
# If something goes wrong, swap back to roll back instantly

blocks.text: Azure App Service stores configuration in Application Settings and Connection Strings. These are injected as environment variables into your application at runtime, overriding appsettings.json values. This is where you store secrets — database connection strings, API keys, third-party credentials — without committing them to source control.

Connection strings in App Service are encrypted at rest and injected using the standard ASP.NET Core connection string configuration key. Slot settings can be marked as 'sticky' so they do not swap between slots — essential for keeping production and staging databases separate.

Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) automates the process of building, testing, and deploying your application whenever code changes. Azure App Service integrates with GitHub Actions, providing a pre-built workflow that triggers on every push to your main branch.

blocks.title: GitHub Actions Workflow for Azure Deployment
blocks.content: A GitHub Actions YAML workflow that builds and deploys an ASP.NET Core app to Azure App Service on every push to main.
blocks.code:
name: Build and Deploy to Azure

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build-and-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up .NET
        uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with:
          dotnet-version: '8.0.x'

      - name: Restore dependencies
        run: dotnet restore MyApp.csproj

      - name: Build
        run: dotnet build MyApp.csproj --configuration Release --no-restore

      - name: Test
        run: dotnet test MyApp.csproj --configuration Release --no-build

      - name: Publish
        run: dotnet publish MyApp.csproj --configuration Release --output ./publish

      - name: Deploy to Azure Web App
        uses: azure/webapps-deploy@v3
        with:
          app-name: MyWebApp12345
          slot-name: staging
          publish-profile: ${{ secrets.AZURE_WEBAPP_PUBLISH_PROFILE }}
          package: ./publish

terms.definition: A managed cloud platform for hosting web applications, APIs, and mobile backends with built-in scaling and SSL.
A logical container in Azure that groups related resources for management, billing, and access control.
Defines the compute resources (CPU, memory, pricing tier) for one or more Azure App Service apps.
A staging environment for an Azure Web App that can be swapped with production for zero-downtime releases.
An Azure deployment method that uploads a ZIP file of your published application and deploys it directly.

blocks.title: Always Use Deployment Slots for Production
blocks.text: Deploying directly to production is risky. Use a staging slot to validate the deployment before swapping. If something goes wrong after the swap, you can swap back to the previous version in seconds.

blocks.title: Lesson Summary: Cloud Deployment
points: Azure App Service is a managed PaaS platform that handles infrastructure, runtime, and scaling for you
Azure CLI scripts make your deployment reproducible and suitable for automation
App Service Plans define compute resources — multiple apps can share one plan to reduce cost
Deployment slots provide zero-downtime releases with instant rollback via slot swapping
Application Settings and Connection Strings inject configuration as environment variables at runtime
GitHub Actions automate CI/CD — build, test, and deploy on every code change without manual steps
blocks.takeaway: Cloud deployment removes the operational burden from your team. Azure App Service handles servers, runtime updates, SSL, and scaling. Combined with deployment slots and CI/CD, you can ship code confidently and roll back instantly if something breaks.

blocks.title: Exercise: Deploy to Azure App Service with a Staging Slot
blocks.description: Provision an Azure App Service instance and deploy an application using a staging slot for safe releases.
steps: Authenticate with Azure using az login
Create a resource group named Quotient-RG in the East US region
Create a Linux App Service Plan named Quotient-Plan in the B1 tier
Create a Web App named quotient-api-[your-initials] with .NET 8 runtime
Publish your ASP.NET Core app locally using dotnet publish
Create a ZIP file of the published output and deploy it using az webapp deploy
Create a staging deployment slot and deploy a code change to it first
Swap the staging slot into production and confirm the app is live
blocks.expectedOutcome: A live ASP.NET Core API running on Azure App Service. A staging slot was used to validate the deployment before swapping to production. The app is accessible via its Azure-provided URL.

items.hint: A resource group holds related resources. An App Service Plan defines compute. A Web App runs your code.

items.hint: az group create, az appservice plan create, az webapp create.

items.text: I understand what deployment slots are and why they matter
items.hint: Slots are staging environments. Deploy to staging, test, then swap with zero downtime.

items.text: I know the difference between ZIP deploy and Git deploy
items.hint: ZIP deploy uploads a packaged artifact. Git deploy pushes source code for the platform to build.

items.hint: A GitHub Actions workflow builds, tests, and deploys automatically on every push to the main branch.
